Separately, the Iran-backed Houthis are increasing pressure on government positions around Aden, Yemen’s interim capital. Saudi-backed government forces said they had pulled back from their Bab el-Mandeb offensive in order to concentrate on defending Aden.
items.cav: The sources do not say whether the drones caused any damage, and the tanker sinking is a Revolutionary Guards claim that has not been independently verified. One part of the reporting mentions a strike on Tehran, but the rest of the account describes strikes on Bahrain and Iranian coastal and naval sites, so the details of that strike are unclear.
items.op: Condemning an attack on a neighbouring state is right, but the principle of international law must apply to every side. US strikes on Iranian sites and Iranian claims about mines both need scrutiny. Claims that shape the war, including the tanker sinking, should be verified independently before they are repeated as fact.

items.t: ASEAN offers Myanmar’s sidelined leaders a phased route back to summits, tied to peace-plan progress
items.s: Southeast Asian leaders have agreed to re-engage Myanmar’s government step by step, but a full return to high-level meetings hinges on advances in a regional peace plan. Fighting continues across the country.
p: Myanmar still belongs to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, yet its political figures have been kept out of summits and foreign ministers’ gatherings since 2021, when the army took power and removed the elected administration headed by Aung San Suu Kyi. The takeover set off a civil war that has not ended.

According to a joint statement issued by the leaders, the bloc could slowly restore Myanmar’s complete political representation if it shows lasting and tangible headway on its five-point peace plan. The approach is designed to move in stages and to respond to what is happening inside the country.

Critics of the plan note that it has produced few results since it was adopted, and clashes persist between the military and pro-democracy and ethnic armed groups. Thailand has argued for closer contact since Min Aung Hlaing assumed a civilian presidency this year, after a vote that monitors rejected as a sham.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. put the question directly at the leaders’ retreat in Manila, asking what more the group could offer Myanmar. He called for workable steps to move the peace plan forward and to back a process that is inclusive and led by Myanmar itself.

The agenda also covers trade, regional security and coordinated fuel supply arrangements, as the war in Iran has disrupted energy flows. Separately, Australia and the Philippines signed a defence pact on Sunday, and Canada and the Philippines said on Saturday they had wrapped up free trade talks.

A draft code of conduct for the South China Sea is still unfinished. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro put the ASEAN–China negotiations at 80% complete, though diplomats told AFP that a deal was unlikely in Manila. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is representing Beijing at the gathering.

US President Donald Trump is expected to join late in the summit on Tuesday and hold meetings with leaders of India, Japan and Australia, the other Quad members. Activists plan to protest that day, partly over a US-backed industrial project north of Manila that they say could push Indigenous families from their land. The Philippines will pass the rotating ASEAN chair to Singapore next year, with Thailand due in 2028.
items.cav: The sources do not define what counts as progress on the peace plan or set a timeline for restoring Myanmar’s representation. Trump’s planned meetings are reported as expectations, not confirmed outcomes. The 80% figure comes from the Philippine foreign secretary, while diplomats doubted a deal was near.
items.op: Tying Myanmar’s return to a peace plan that has delivered little since 2021 risks turning engagement into a holding pattern. Staged re-entry can be pragmatic, but it must come with measurable benchmarks and public reporting. Otherwise ASEAN rewards the coup leadership without any accountable result.

items.t: US pitch would tie Ukraine’s NATO membership to giving up Donbas, Zelenskyy says
items.s: Washington has reportedly proposed a route into NATO for Ukraine on condition that Kyiv cede the Donbas region, a demand Russia has made as a condition for ending the war. Kyiv has not accepted the idea.
p: The United States has floated a new pathway for Ukraine to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, an aspiration Kyiv has pursued since applying in September 2022, roughly a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the proposal would require Ukraine to give up the whole of the Donbas region in the east.

Zelenskyy said the idea was conveyed to him by Trump’s negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, during the latest US-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. The two envoys then met Vladimir Putin in Moscow, before briefing Zelenskyy in Dublin ahead of a meeting of European leaders there. The account of the offer comes from Zelenskyy; the sources reviewed do not include a direct public statement from the US envoys.

Zelenskyy told reporters that the Americans had asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from Donbas if it joined NATO. He described the question as part of an “extremely difficult” conversation that would shape European security, and said that NATO was “back on the agenda”. He also said the idea of trading territory for NATO membership had not previously been raised by alliance members.

Kyiv’s position, as restated by Zelenskyy, is that it will not give up any of its territory. He said that if a deal included security guarantees, the right to keep a strong, well-funded army and funds to rebuild the country, he would hold a national referendum on ceding territory in exchange for NATO membership. Russia’s stance is that Ukrainian membership would bring a “harsh response”, and Putin has demanded that NATO pull back forces from countries bordering Russia.

Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera were sceptical. Ian Lesser of the German Marshall Fund said the proposal, if accurate, clearly reflects a long-held view in US administration circles that Ukraine should make territorial concessions. He added that it was hard to imagine Moscow agreeing to the NATO element, and that some alliance members would also be doubtful. Chris Featherstone of the University of York called the idea a major departure from earlier US positions, given Trump’s repeated criticism of NATO and his public dispute with Zelenskyy, and questioned whether Trump could bring other allies on board.

NATO members remain divided on offering Ukraine membership during an ongoing war, although most agree on strong support for Kyiv. Featherstone suggested the proposal may be an attempt to test Ukraine’s refusal to cede land, rather than a settled plan. Whether the offer is genuine, and whether any of the parties would accept it, remains unclear from the reporting available.
items.cav: The core claim about the US offer rests mainly on Zelenskyy’s account of private talks; the envoys’ own words are not quoted in the sources. Analysts describe the proposal as possibly inaccurate or a test, and no sources confirm the Kremlin’s response to the NATO element.
items.op: A peace settlement that trades a sovereign nation’s territory for its own security guarantees would reward the invader and undermine the principle that borders cannot be redrawn by force. Any deal touching Donbas should be made in public, with its terms open to scrutiny by Ukrainians and by NATO’s members, not negotiated behind closed doors.

items.t: SpaceX catches upper part of Starship rocket on return to Earth in first-ever attempt
items.s: SpaceX caught the upper part of its Starship rocket between mechanical arms as it returned to Earth on Saturday, a first for a spaceship, according to reports from Euronews and the BBC. The same launch also saw the booster fail to return to the launch site.
p: According to Euronews, the upper section came back to Earth on Saturday and was caught between two mechanical “chopstick” arms at Starbase in Texas. The BBC reported the same achievement and said the arms are nicknamed chopsticks.

Starship lifted off from Starbase on Friday and orbited Earth 14 times, deploying 26 satellites for Elon Musk’s Starlink internet constellation, Euronews reported. After a journey of about 22 hours, the craft approached Texas’ east coast, and its three Raptor engines ignited as it descended toward the launchpad.

SpaceX celebrated the result on social media. Musk wrote on X that he had “hugged ship 42” upon its return. Crowds at the site cheered as the arms closed around the spacecraft for the first time, a moment the company said “changed everything.”

The BBC said the ship returned at around 15:20 local time, a few minutes behind schedule. Euronews noted that spaceships had previously been single-use vehicles, which made each launch particularly expensive. Starship is also lined up to serve as a landing system for NASA’s Artemis Moon landing mission.

The day was not a clean sweep. SpaceX had hoped to catch both the booster and the upper stage. The booster’s catch was aborted minutes after launch. SpaceX said its guidance system triggered an automated abort and the booster diverted to an offshore landing, and that the boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass. The company said the root cause was under investigation. The BBC described the booster as diverted to the ocean and bursting into flames just above the sea.
items.cav: The two outlets describe the booster’s fate differently: Euronews reports an offshore splashdown in the Gulf, while the BBC says it burst into flames just above the sea. The cause of the booster fault is still under investigation, and the sources do not explain it. The praise from SpaceX and Musk is company and personal commentary, not independent verification.
items.op: A catch of a returning spacecraft is a real engineering milestone, but celebration should not replace scrutiny. SpaceX should publish a full analysis of the booster failure, including its timeline and fuel data, so outside observers can judge what went wrong. Transparency, not spectacle, is what turns a test flight into lasting progress.

items.t: Copper wire upgrade behind US flight shutdown, transport secretary says
items.s: A nationwide US ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights was caused by a technical problem during a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy has said. The government is still trying to establish the root cause.
p: Air traffic controllers suspended take-offs across the United States for four hours on Friday, a move that led to thousands of cancellations and widespread travel disruption. Duffy told a news conference that the problem followed work to upgrade the system.

Duffy said the government was trying to determine whether the failure resulted from “incompetence” by the company carrying out the upgrades or from faulty equipment. Officials, including Duffy, had earlier blamed outdated equipment.

According to Duffy, a contractor, the technology provider L3Harris, was switching air traffic control systems from copper wire to fibre-optic cable. He described the US telecommunications system as very old, saying the type of wire involved was being discontinued.

Duffy explained that a router being worked on had begun flooding other air traffic control systems and caused communication problems with aircraft. Authorities then halted take-offs on safety grounds. The government is now examining whether the wire replacement or the router fault was the root cause.

The ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, but its effects carried into Saturday as airlines worked to clear a backlog. Flight tracking data cited by the BBC suggested more than 15,000 US flights were delayed or cancelled on Friday, affecting an estimated 1.5 million passengers. On Saturday, more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and 7,000 delayed. Some flights from the UK and Europe were also cancelled. The Federal Aviation Administration said the schedule should return to normal by the end of Sunday.

US officials said they did not believe a cyber-attack was responsible. FAA head Bryan Bedford said there was “zero evidence” of anything nefarious, though Duffy said the investigation into the exact cause was still under way. L3Harris said it had completed more than 70% of its assigned modernisation work before the shutdown and was supporting the FAA’s inquiry.

Duffy warned that a similar failure could happen again unless Congress approves upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure. President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for those upgrades, and Republicans control both chambers of Congress.
items.cav: The cause is not yet established: the sources report that the government is still weighing the wire replacement against a router fault, and that the contractor’s role has not been confirmed by any finding. Disruption figures come from flight tracking data and an estimate of passenger numbers, not an official tally. The FAA’s view that no cyber-attack was involved is reported as an official position, and the investigation’s conclusions have not been published.
items.op: Four hours of grounded flights should prompt more than reassurance. The public deserves a clear, published account of whether a contractor’s work, ageing equipment or both caused the failure, and of what Congress will fund. Safety systems demand transparency, and officials who promise upgrades should be held to them.

items.t: US judge temporarily blocks Trump’s plan to overhaul historic Washington golf course
items.s: A federal judge has temporarily halted a plan to close and redevelop a historic public golf course in Washington, another setback for President Donald Trump’s effort to turn it into a championship-level course.
p: Judge Ana Reyes issued a 30-page decision on Saturday that pauses the federal government’s plan to shut East Potomac Park, which was due to close from 15 November for renovations. The park lies near the Jefferson Memorial, about two miles south of the White House.

Trump announced in October that the course would be rebuilt over 15 months into a facility that is open to the public yet designed to a very high standard and able to host major tournaments. He has described the existing layout as worn out, with dangerous trees and a failing seawall.

Reyes found that the administration’s explanations for the closure were “pretextual,” and concluded that officials had breached at least two federal laws “to meet an arbitrary deadline.” In her words, the government was seeking to shut a historic park that residents across the city use every day, with no end date.

The order keeps the park open, but it does not require the administration to keep golf running there. Reyes did add, however, that officials may not treat the lack of golf as grounds for barring visitors.

The DC Preservation League brought the case, arguing that the redevelopment breaks federal rules and statutes. Earlier, Reyes stopped the National Park Service from felling trees or making permanent changes without advance warning, after hundreds of trees had come down on short notice. Democracy Forward, which represents the group, welcomed the latest ruling.

The litigation has also grown acrimonious. Reyes has opened an ethics inquiry into whether government lawyers repeatedly misled her about the closure timeline, while the Justice Department has accused her of exceeding her authority and has asked her to step aside. She refused. The Interior Department, Justice Department and White House did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

At present the park offers three golf courses with 36 holes in total, a miniature golf course and a paved loop frequented by cyclists and runners. The plan would replace all of that with one 18-hole championship layout, which Trump has suggested could stage events such as the US Open and the Ryder Cup.
items.cav: The sources differ on timing: an NPR summary describes a two-week delay, while the Guardian and BBC reports do not give a duration for the block. The reporting also relies on the judge’s written decision as quoted by outlets, and the White House had not responded at the time of publication.
items.op: Courts are doing what the public should expect when a government moves quickly and skips notice: it must justify itself on the record. Transparency about why a public park is closed matters more than who wins the golf course. The pointed question is why the administration rushed past its own legal duties.

items.t: Zelenskyy says US asked whether Ukraine would leave Donbas for Nato membership
items.s: Kyiv’s president says Washington has asked whether Ukraine would give up part of the Donbas in return for joining Nato. He says he will not hand over territory, but would take a deal to a referendum if security guarantees and funding came with it.
p: In remarks to reporters, released by his office on Saturday, Zelenskyy said US officials had for the first time put a question to Kyiv: would Ukraine pull back from areas of the eastern Donbas that Russian forces do not hold, if it were admitted to Nato? He said the query showed that the alliance was back on the table.

He warned that such an arrangement, which could form part of a wider postwar security order for Europe, might let Moscow weaken Nato and redraw frontiers. In his view, steps of that kind tend to bring about wars or escalation. The report does not explain how the American side framed the idea.

Zelenskyy held that Ukraine is not prepared to cede land. However, he said he would let voters decide in a national referendum if the country were offered a full package: security guarantees, a robust and well-financed army, and money to rebuild. He also ruled out neutrality, which he said would require changing the constitution, and noted that Ukraine is not in Nato at present.

He pushed back on Moscow’s demand that a broad European security agreement come first, before the terms for ending the fighting are set. His stance echoed that of European leaders who met in Dublin on Friday. In his words, the war has to end before anything else is reshaped.

Jared Kushner, the envoy and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, said on Saturday that Washington is working to bring Russia and European governments into direct talks. That followed trilateral meetings among the US, Russia and Ukraine earlier in the week, which reportedly produced an agreement that European countries will take part in future negotiations. Neither Washington nor Nato had publicly responded to the Donbas-for-membership idea.

Separately, Zelenskyy accused SpaceX of being untruthful about limits on Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system. He called the speed restrictions, in place for five days, political rather than technical. Ukrainian drones, he said, can no longer intercept incoming jet-powered Shahed drones. Kyiv suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US move to press him into concessions to Putin, and the report includes no reply from SpaceX.

Macron posted on social media that those seeking to cut aid to Ukraine are effectively trying to impose an unjust peace on Kyiv and, by extension, on Europe, which he described as a path to another war. Elsewhere, Russia’s defence ministry, quoted by the RIA news agency, said it had hit a cargo ship at the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk that was supplying the Ukrainian military. Ukraine’s General Staff said its strikes set oil storage tanks ablaze at the Samara pipeline station, a key node in Russia’s oil export network, and Ukraine’s Emergency Service reported 22 people injured in a Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia.
items.cav: The account of the US question comes solely from Zelenskyy, and Washington and Nato had not commented, so the American position remains unconfirmed. The Russian claim about the cargo vessel and the SpaceX allegations are also one-sided, and the report does not give the other sides’ full responses.
items.op: Any deal trading Ukrainian land for a security promise should be made in the open, with affected people given a say. Zelenskyy’s referendum offer is the right instinct, but it means something only if the terms are public and the process honest. Quiet bargaining over borders risks the same war under a new name.

items.t: Italy fines Meta €805m over Android users’ photo access without specific consent
items.s: Italy’s data protection authority has fined Meta €805m, or about $887m, for accessing photos and videos on Android devices through the Facebook app without specific consent. Meta says it will appeal.
p: Italy’s data protection authority has fined Meta €805m (about $887m) for accessing photos and videos from Android users without their specific consent. The regulator said the Facebook app gave Meta access to images, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users, and that people were not properly informed about this.

According to the authority, roughly 20 million smartphone users in Italy were affected. The regulator said they were not made aware that the app could reach their photo galleries, a point it linked to a single app-wide authorisation that came after a notice asking users to enable other features.

The case concerns a feature, available since 2023, that suggests photos and videos from a user’s phone gallery as ideas for posts while they browse. The regulator said that Facebook’s notice did not make clear that the permission would also allow those suggestions to be generated.

In setting the size of the penalty, the authority said it weighed the large number of people affected and the length of the breach, which it said was still continuing for users who had not updated the app or who had already agreed to the system. It also cited what it called Meta’s lack of cooperation during the investigation.

The regulator has ordered Meta to change how the feature works. According to the BBC, the company has 60 days to disable it by default and to seek users’ consent through a separate request. Under the requirements described, Meta must also clearly explain what the feature does and how to switch it off.

Meta responded that it “strongly disagree[s]” with the regulator’s assessment and with the level of the fine. In a statement given to the BBC, the company said the feature helps people post photos and videos and that users must grant permission on their device before it can operate.

The Guardian reported that the fine is roughly 0.4% of the group’s annual turnover, which it put at $201bn in 2025. It also reported that the penalty is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a technology company, below a 2021 fine of more than €1.1bn against Amazon for breaching competition law.

Both outlets also referred to a separate case in the United States. The BBC said a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn after finding that the company had misled the public about how it handled user data. The Guardian described the order as coming from authorities in New Mexico, a difference in wording that the sources do not explain.
items.cav: The sources differ on who imposed the New Mexico penalty, with the BBC saying a judge ordered it and the Guardian saying authorities did. Meta’s account of the feature is its own and has not been independently tested, and the reports do not say whether the appeal will suspend the fine.
items.op: Users should not have to discover by accident that an app can reach their private photo library. Meta’s argument that permission exists in device settings misses the point: consent has to be specific and understood, not buried in a bundled prompt. The regulator’s insistence on clear notice and a fresh opt-in is the minimum transparency that large platforms owe their users.

items.t: Official works two NFL games after nationwide FAA halt upends weekend sports travel
items.s: A nationwide Federal Aviation Administration flight halt on Friday forced leagues and clubs across the United States to reshuffle officials and travel plans. Some of the knock-on effects were still visible on Sunday.
p: Don Willard, an NFL official, is set to work two games on Sunday. The FAA’s nationwide halt on Friday, which lasted several hours, put his original plans in doubt. He is due to call the Miami Dolphins against the Indianapolis Colts at 1pm ET, then drive 112 miles east to officiate the Pittsburgh Steelers against the Cincinnati Bengals on Sunday Night Football.
Because NFL teams generally travel the day before a game, the league’s Sunday slate absorbed much of the shock. Still, the stoppage required changes to officiating crews across the league.

The NBA also had to adjust its referee assignments as travel problems lingered into Saturday. Brian Forte took a place in the Chicago-Minnesota crew, succeeding Jason Goldenberg, while Jenna Schroeder moved into the Dallas-Cleveland game in Forte’s spot. In Brooklyn-Memphis, Michael Smith was added to the three-person crew late in the afternoon because another referee could not reach the arena in time. Later on Saturday, Brent Barnaky and CJ Washington were assigned to Denver-New Orleans.

Sport returned gradually to its usual rhythm on Saturday, though clubs were still coping with the aftermath. Many college football sides arrived the day before kickoff, and several fixtures were held back by hours so that visiting squads could get in and prepare. Utah’s trip to Arizona and Arizona State’s trip to Central Florida were both delayed three hours, while Auburn chose charter buses. The one notable exception was Mississippi’s No 19 game at Oklahoma, which was switched to Sunday with a 1pm ET start.

Other sports felt it too. The Southern California women’s basketball squad was taken off its aircraft and spent the night in Los Angeles, setting off for Greenville only on Saturday afternoon. Fairleigh Dickinson learned late on Friday that its flight to Ohio State had been scrapped, and coach Stephanie Gaitley opted for a 10-hour coach journey on Saturday morning rather than an overnight departure. The Kansas City Current told ESPN they were working with the NWSL and their charter operator to reach their Sunday semi-final in New York in time. Most of the 14 NHL fixtures on Saturday were largely untouched, since the majority of clubs had already landed, though the San Jose Sharks did not arrive in Utah until late Friday.

The Cleveland Cavaliers faced the most severe NBA disruption. Unable to fly out of Miami on Friday night, they departed at 8.54am on Saturday to meet the Dallas Mavericks that evening. Donovan Mitchell said he would rather have seen the game moved, but said the squad would “make adjustments” and push on. A reschedule was impractical, given that the Cleveland arena hosts events on 11 straight days. The club listed Mitchell, James Harden, Peyton Watson and Jarrett Allen as questionable, and all four had started Friday’s game in Miami.
items.cav: The sources do not explain what triggered the FAA halt or give more detail than “several hours”. Willard’s Sunday logistics and the Cavaliers’ injury status come from press reporting rather than official league statements, and the Current’s remarks are the club’s own account.
items.op: Leagues absorbed this disruption quietly, but a federal flight halt should not leave fans and players guessing. The FAA and the leagues owe the public a clear account of what went wrong and what contingency plans exist. Without one, the next stoppage will be met with the same improvisation.
